q: Structures I and II are the two resonance contributors of the methoxymethyl cation. Which statement is correct?
c: II is the major contributor because every atom has a complete octet
I is the major contributor because the positive charge is on the less electronegative carbon
I and II contribute equally because they are equivalent structures
II is not a valid contributor because oxygen cannot carry a positive charge
h: Rank contributors by the octet rule first; charge placement on the more or less electronegative atom is a later tiebreaker.
w: The first criterion for the major contributor is that the most atoms have full octets. In II every C and O has an octet (O has three bonds and one lone pair, +1). In I the CH2+ carbon has only six electrons. So II is the major contributor, even though it puts + on oxygen. This oxygen stabilization is why α-alkoxy carbocations (oxocarbenium ions) form easily.
x: Charge placement is only a tiebreaker between structures with equal numbers of octets; I has an electron-deficient carbon, so it is the minor contributor.
The two structures are not equivalent: they differ in octets and in where the charge sits, so they do not contribute equally.
Oxygen often carries +1 (hydronium, protonated alcohols, oxonium ions); with three bonds and one lone pair, + is the correct formal charge.

q: Rank the three resonance contributors of N,N-dimethylacetamide from least to most important (stable).
h: Use the rules in order: full octets first, then fewest formal charges.
w: I has full octets and no formal charges, so it is the most important. II has full octets but separated charges (N+, O−), so it is next. III also has separated charges and a carbon with only six electrons, so it is least important. Order: III < II < I. II is still a significant contributor, which is why amides are planar with a short C–N bond.
x: II has an octet at every atom while III has an electron-deficient carbon, so II is more important than III.
Charge separation makes II and III less stable than neutral I; I is the most important contributor, not the least.
Neutral I with all octets outranks charge-separated II; the octet rule and fewest charges both favor I.

q: Which carbocation is stabilized by resonance?
h: Resonance needs the empty p orbital directly next to a π bond, with the orbitals parallel.
w: The but-3-en-2-yl cation is allylic: the cationic carbon is directly bonded to the C=C, so the π electrons can shift to give a second contributor with + on the terminal CH2. In the homoallylic cation an sp3 CH2 separates the π bond from the cation. In the vinyl cation the empty orbital lies in the plane of the molecule, perpendicular to the C=C π bond, so no overlap is possible. The sec-butyl cation has no π bond at all.
x: The CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> is one carbon removed from the alkene; with an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon in between, the π bond cannot overlap with the empty p orbital.
In a vinyl cation the empty orbital is perpendicular to the C=C π bond, so the two cannot overlap; vinyl cations are especially unstable.
The sec-butyl cation is stabilized only by hyperconjugation and induction; it has no π bond to delocalize the charge.

q: How many significant resonance contributors (including the one shown) can be drawn for the anion of pentane-2,4-dione?
h: The lone pair on the central carbon can push into either C=O bond.
w: The central carbanion can delocalize into the left C=O (putting − on that oxygen) or the right C=O (putting − on the other oxygen). With the drawn carbanion form that is 3 contributors, two of which place the charge on an electronegative oxygen. This extra delocalization is why the C3–H of pentane-2,4-dione has pKa ≈ 9, far lower than a simple ketone (about 19).
x: Two contributors would describe a simple ketone enolate; here there are two carbonyls, so the charge can reach either oxygen.
There is no fourth reasonable contributor: the CH<sub>3</sub> groups and C=O carbons have no further π bonds or lone pairs to shift.
Five would require moving σ bonds or hydrogens, which changes the compound rather than drawing a resonance form.

q: Number the cation below C1 (the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon) through C6 (the CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> carbon). Considering all of its resonance contributors, which carbons share the positive charge?
c: C2, C3, C4, C5 and C6
h: Push one π bond at a time toward the cationic carbon and see where the + moves each time.
w: Moving the C4=C5 π electrons toward C6 forms C5=C6 and puts + on C4. Then moving the C2=C3 π electrons toward C4 forms C3=C4 and puts + on C2. So the charge is shared by C2, C4 and C6: in a conjugated cation the + appears on alternating carbons, never on two adjacent ones.
x: This skips the middle contributor; you cannot get from + at C6 to + at C2 without passing through + at C4.
Charge in a conjugated π system alternates; C3 and C5 always keep a π bond in every contributor and never carry the +.
C3 and C5 keep a π bond in every contributor, so they are exactly the carbons that never bear the charge.

q:
Consider the acetate ion.
I. The two C–O bonds have the same length.
II. Each oxygen carries about half of the negative charge.
III. The ion rapidly flips back and forth between its two resonance contributors.
Which statements are true?
h: A resonance hybrid is a single real structure, not a mixture of structures in equilibrium.
w: Acetate has two equivalent contributors, so the real ion is their average: both C–O bonds are equal (about 1.26 Å, between C=O and C–O) and each oxygen carries about −½. Statement III describes resonance incorrectly: contributors are not separate species interconverting; the hybrid exists all the time. Answer: I and II only.
x: II is also true: equivalent contributors share the charge equally, so each O is about −½.
III is the classic misconception; the ion never exists as either contributor, so nothing flips.
III is false; resonance contributors are imaginary pictures, and the actual ion is always the hybrid.

q: Which structure is a resonance contributor of protonated acetone (shown), rather than a different compound?
h: All four have the formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. Resonance forms may move only π electrons and lone pairs; every atom, including every H, must stay put.
w: Moving the C=O π electrons onto oxygen gives (CH3)2C+–OH: the same atoms with the same connections, only electrons moved. Each of the other structures has a hydrogen or a carbon in a new place, so each is a constitutional isomer. The real ion is a hybrid with + shared between C and O, which explains why acid makes a carbonyl carbon more electrophilic.
x: Here a hydrogen has moved from a CH<sub>3</sub> to the central carbon; changing where an H is attached makes a different compound, not a resonance form.
This is the O-protonated enol (a tautomer pathway): an H moved from carbon to oxygen, so it is a different compound.
Oxygen is now on a terminal carbon and a hydrogen has moved, so this is a constitutional isomer (a cation derived from propan-1-ol), not a form of protonated acetone.

q: Structures I and II are resonance contributors of the enolate of acetone. Which statement is correct?
c: II is the major contributor because the negative charge is on the more electronegative oxygen
I is the major contributor because a negative charge is more stable on carbon
I and II contribute equally because both have full octets
Neither is valid, because I and II differ in the position of a hydrogen
h: Both have full octets and one formal charge. Use the tiebreaker: where is a negative charge most comfortable?
w: Both contributors obey the octet rule and each has a single −1 charge. The tiebreaker is electronegativity: a negative charge is better on the more electronegative atom, so II (the oxyanion) is the major contributor. Most of the charge density sits on oxygen, though the carbon still reacts as a nucleophile because its HOMO coefficient is large.
x: Carbon is less electronegative than oxygen, so it holds negative charge less well; I is the minor contributor.
Equal octets do not mean equal weight; charge location breaks the tie in favor of oxygen.
No hydrogen moves between I and II; only the π electrons and a lone pair shift, so they are valid resonance forms.

q: In the phenoxide ion, on which tagged ring carbons does the negative charge appear in resonance contributors?
h: Push an oxygen lone pair into the ring and follow the charge around one double bond at a time.
w: An O lone pair forms C=O, and the ring π bond moves to put − on the ortho carbon (a). Shifting the next π bond moves the charge to the para carbon (c), then to the other ortho carbon. The meta carbons (b) never carry the charge, because charge moves to alternating atoms. Answer: a and c.
x: The meta position is the one carbon type that never receives the charge.
Charge in a conjugated system alternates; it skips the meta carbon b.
Carbon b is meta and never bears the charge; the para carbon c does.

q: Based on resonance, which tagged carbons of pent-3-en-2-one carry a partial positive charge?
h: Draw the contributor with C<sup>+</sup>–O<sup>−</sup>, then move the C=C π bond toward the cation.
w: Polarizing the C=O gives + on the carbonyl carbon a. The adjacent C=C π electrons can shift to form a C=C between a and b, leaving + on the β-carbon c. So both a and c are electrophilic, which is why α,β-unsaturated carbonyls accept nucleophiles at the β-carbon (conjugate addition).
x: The β-carbon c also gets a + in a contributor; this is the basis of conjugate (1,4-) addition.
The α-carbon b never carries the + charge; charge alternates and skips it.
Carbon a, the carbonyl carbon, is δ+, and b is not.

q: In methyl acetate, rank the three bonds from shortest to longest: I = a–b, II = a–c, III = c–d.
h: A double bond is shortest. Then compare the two C–O single bonds: one has partial double-bond character from resonance and an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, the other does not.
w: I is the C=O double bond (about 1.20 Å). II, the acyl C–O bond, is shortened because the ester oxygen's lone pair donates into the C=O (a contributor with C=O+–CH3) and because the carbon is sp2 (about 1.34 Å). III, the O–CH3 bond, is an ordinary single bond to an sp3 carbon (about 1.44 Å). Order: I < II < III.
x: The acyl C–O bond (II) has partial double-bond character from resonance, so it is shorter, not longer, than the O–CH<sub>3</sub> bond.
A C=O double bond is shorter than any C–O bond with only partial double-bond character.
This is the reverse order; the full double bond I is the shortest.

q: In the allyl anion as drawn, the carbon bearing the negative charge is best described as:
c: sp<sup>2</sup>, with the lone pair in a p orbital that is part of the π system
sp<sup>3</sup>, with the lone pair in an sp<sup>3</sup> orbital
sp, with the lone pair in an sp orbital
sp<sup>2</sup>, with the lone pair in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital in the plane of the molecule
h: A lone pair next to a π bond is delocalized only if it sits in an orbital parallel to the π bond.
w: Because the lone pair can delocalize onto the other terminal carbon, the charged carbon rehybridizes to sp2 and places the lone pair in a p orbital that overlaps with the C=C π bond. All three carbons are then sp2, and the two terminal carbons share the negative charge equally. Rule: an atom with a lone pair adjacent to a π bond uses a p orbital for that lone pair.
x: Counting domains as drawn (three bonds + one lone pair) gives sp<sup>3</sup>, but that ignores resonance; an sp<sup>3</sup> lone pair could not overlap with the π bond.
The carbon has three σ bonds, so it needs three hybrid orbitals; sp would leave too few.
A lone pair in an in-plane sp<sup>2</sup> orbital would be perpendicular to the π bond and could not be delocalized.

q: Which statement about nitromethane is correct?
c: The two N–O bonds have the same length, between that of an N–O single bond and an N=O double bond
Nitrogen is +1 in one resonance contributor and neutral in the other
The best Lewis structure has two N=O double bonds and no formal charges
The negative charge stays on one oxygen while the other oxygen remains neutral
h: Draw the second contributor by swapping which oxygen has the double bond. Are the two structures equivalent?
w: Nitromethane has two equivalent contributors that differ only in which oxygen holds the double bond. N is +1 in both, and each O is −½ in the hybrid. So the two N–O bonds are identical (about 1.22 Å) with a bond order of about 1.5.
x: N has four bonds and no lone pairs in both contributors, so it is +1 in each.
Two N=O bonds would give N five bonds (10 electrons); second-row atoms cannot exceed an octet.
Because the two contributors are equivalent, the negative charge is shared equally by both oxygens.

q: Methyl azide is often drawn as CH<sub>3</sub>–N=N<sup>+</sup>=N<sup>−</sup> (shown). In the other octet contributor, CH<sub>3</sub>–N–N≡N (N1 bonded to CH<sub>3</sub>), what are the formal charges on N1, N2 and N3?
h: Give each N an octet in CH<sub>3</sub>–N–N≡N, then use valence − nonbonding − ½ bonding.
w: In CH3–N–N≡N, N1 has two bonds and two lone pairs: 5 − 4 − 2 = −1. N2 has four bonds and no lone pairs: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. N3 has three bonds and one lone pair: 5 − 2 − 3 = 0. The middle nitrogen of an azide is +1 in every octet contributor, while the −1 charge moves between N1 and N3.
x: These are the charges in the contributor that was drawn, not the triple-bonded one; moving electrons shifts the −1 from N3 to N1.
N2 has four bonds and no lone pair in both contributors, so it is always +1, and N3 with a triple bond and a lone pair is 0.
N1 has two lone pairs and two bonds, which makes it −1, and N2 with four bonds is +1.

q: Which set of curved arrows converts the oxyanion contributor of the acetone enolate (shown) into the carbanion contributor?
c: One arrow from an O lone pair to the C–O bond, and one from the C=C π bond onto the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon
One arrow from an O lone pair directly to the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon
One arrow from the C=C π bond to the C–O bond, and one from an O lone pair onto the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon
One arrow from a C–H σ bond of the CH<sub>3</sub> to the C–O bond
h: Arrows start at electrons (lone pairs or π bonds) and end where those electrons become a new bond or lone pair. Make sure no carbon ends up with five bonds.
w: The O lone pair moves in to make the C=O π bond (arrow 1, lone pair → C–O bond). The central carbon would then have five bonds, so the C=C π bond must leave as a lone pair on the CH2 carbon (arrow 2, π bond → CH2). This gives CH3C(=O)CH2−. Resonance arrows move only π electrons and lone pairs.
x: Electrons cannot jump across an atom to a non-adjacent atom; the charge is relayed by two arrows through the central carbon.
The arrows' origins are swapped: the C=C π electrons cannot go to oxygen's bond while the O lone pair goes to a distant carbon.
Resonance never breaks σ bonds; moving a C–H σ bond would change the structure (a different compound), not draw a resonance form.

q: Which statement about the guanidinium ion (shown) is correct?
c: It has three equivalent resonance contributors, so all three C–N bonds have the same length
It has two resonance contributors, and the positive charge rests on carbon in the major one
One C–N bond is a double bond and is shorter than the other two C–N bonds
The two NH<sub>2</sub> nitrogens are sp<sup>3</sup> because each has a localized lone pair
h: Each NH<sub>2</sub> lone pair is next to the C=N bond. How many ways can you place the double bond?
w: The C=N+ can be drawn to any of the three nitrogens, with the other two NH2 lone pairs adjacent to it. The three contributors are equivalent, so the hybrid has three identical C–N bonds (bond order 1⅓), each N carries about +⅓, and all three nitrogens are sp2 and planar. This exceptional delocalization makes guanidine one of the strongest neutral organic bases (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 13.6).
x: There are three equivalent contributors, and in each one the + is on a nitrogen with four bonds; carbon keeps its octet.
Since all three contributors are equivalent, no single C=N exists in the real ion; all three bonds are the same length.
Each NH<sub>2</sub> lone pair is delocalized into the C=N π system, so those nitrogens are sp<sup>2</sup> with the lone pair in a p orbital.
